title: Book 8 — Urania, Chapter 143
paragraphs: To Alexander the Athenians answered thus: “We ourselves know well enough that the Mede's power is many times greater than ours — there is no need for you to cast this in our teeth. Nevertheless, because we long for liberty, we shall defend ourselves as we can. Do not try to persuade us to make a treaty with the barbarian, for we on our part will not be persuaded. Now report to Mardonius that the Athenians say this: so long as the sun keeps the same course on which he goes now, we will never make an agreement with Xerxes. We shall go forth to defend ourselves against him, trusting the gods and heroes as our allies — whom he had no respect for when he set fire to their houses and sacred images. And in the future do not appear before the Athenians with any such proposals, nor think you are doing them a service by advising them to do what is not lawful. For we do not wish you to suffer anything unpleasant at the hands of the Athenians, being their public guest and friend.”
